1.pericope_label: Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity... Trust in the Lord, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed

schools.summary: Handles the psalm as a designed artefact. Its whole argument is stated in a sentence — do not let the prosperity of the ungodly vex you, since it will suddenly end and the issue decides between righteous and unrighteous — and the form is described: short proverbial utterances following the alphabet, with deliberate repetition to press the thought deeper. The vocabulary is worked in parallel, the verb behind fret meaning to heat or inflame oneself and the word for envy sharing that root, while the grass metaphor, elsewhere a mournful sigh over human weakness, becomes here a comfort.

States the difficulty at its sharpest: the bolder a man's contempt of God the happier he seems, and since prosperity looks like a token of favour one might conclude that the world is governed by chance or that God makes no difference between good and bad. The answer is admitted to be paradoxical and repugnant to human reason — the felicity of the wicked transient and cursed, God's servants never ceasing to be happy in their greatest calamities — and is held to be profitable precisely because it withdraws the mind from the present aspect of things.

Doubts the ascription. The title gives the psalm to David and most versions follow, but it is thought more likely a consoling ode for the captives in Babylon, who had every temptation to envy while idolaters prospered, with the return predicted in no fewer than ten places. The acrostic is described in detail, two verses under each letter with only the first showing it, and its irregularities catalogued. A second voice in this school keeps only the plain application, that the wicked are not to be envied because they prosper in their enterprises.

Begins with the psalmist rather than with the wicked: David preaches this to himself first, communing upon his bed to suppress the passions he found working there, since that is preached best which is first preached to ourselves. The temptation is traced in stages, from what is seen abroad to what is felt within, and fretfulness and envy are called their own punishment. The images are supplied by a second voice — law-breakers riding on horses while obedient subjects walk in the mire, the best meat going to the dogs, and the fat bullock garlanded on its way to the shambles.
Opens elsewhere altogether, on the day whose hour God willed to stay unknown so that the heart might always be ready for what it knows must come.

debates.question: Who wrote this psalm, and for whom?

positions.summary: David, as the title says, out of some great danger of his own.
More probably an ode composed for the Babylonian captives, whose return it repeatedly predicts.

debates.question: What is the psalm's remedy for envy?

positions.summary: Self-examination and self-preaching: the passions are suppressed by turning the argument on one's own heart first.
A corrected view: faith has clearer optics than sight, and seeing the end of the prosperous makes envy impossible.
A doctrine of providence held against appearances, admitted to be repugnant to reason and profitable for that very reason.

outliers.reading: Opens the exposition not on the psalm's counsel about the prosperous wicked but on the unknown hour of the last day, and on why the Son is said not to know what he does not teach.

themes: Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.
For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb.
Trust in the Lord, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.

4.pericope_label: Delight thyself also in the Lord; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart... Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way

schools.summary: Presses the surrender in the second precept to its limit — roll the cares of your life's way onto God, leave its guidance entirely to him, doing nothing yourself — and notes that the Greek mistranslated the verb as uncover. Defines the resting that follows as resignation, a quiet of mind that rests on God and renounces self-help, with the second verb an inward gathering of oneself in hope; a companion voice renders the same imperative as Hush! Be still, and reads the promised vindication against an Eastern dawn climbing to meridian glory.

Spreads the delighting across the persons of God, his perfections, his works, his word and his people. On committing the way it records the alternative renderings, reveal and roll, explains that revealing is not for God's information since it is our duty to ask and his delight to hear, and then refuses the quietist conclusion: the command does not mean that men should sit still and leave everything to be done for them. Guards the resting the same way — not a stupid indolence or a stoical apathy, nor an entire silence, since the afflicted may own the affliction, pray and speak of the goodness found in it.

Takes the verb for committing as rolling a load, from the camel that kneels until its burden is rolled on, and makes the vindication instantaneous — God saying let thy innocence appear as once he said let there be light. Renders the resting as be silent, be dumb, do not find fault with thy Maker, and reads the following reflexive verb as setting oneself to expect God. A second voice reduces the precept to commending one's cares by fervent prayer.

Reads the precepts as a rising staircase from not fretting to trusting to delighting, and draws the odd but exact counsel that one should in a certain sense imitate the wicked, who delight in their portion. Limits the promise attached to the innermost desires rather than casual wishes, on the ground that such a man's will is already subdued. On resting it insists on a submissive rather than a sullen silence, patient bearing joined to patient expectation, and closes on the waiting: time is nothing to God, and there is more of his love in your defeats than in the successes of the wicked.

debates.question: How much does committing one's way to God require a man to stop doing?

positions.summary: Everything: leave the guidance of your life entirely to him and do nothing in it yourself.
Nothing of the sort: men are not to sit still and be inactive, but to seek direction and strength for every business and give God the glory.
The point is transfer of anxiety, not of activity — the ploughman still sows and harrows, and leaves only the harvest to God.

debates.question: How complete is the silence commanded in rest in the Lord?

positions.summary: Total: be silent, be dumb, and find no fault with thy Maker.
Not total: it excludes arraigning and murmuring, not owning the affliction, praying over it, or telling others what goodness was found in it.
An inward posture rather than an outward one — resignation and a gathering of oneself in hope.

outliers.reading: Finds the picture for committing one's way in the camel that lies down until its load is rolled upon it, making the precept an image of accepting a burden rather than shedding one.

themes: Delight thyself also in the Lord; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
Commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday.
Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.

8.pericope_label: Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil... A little that a righteous man hath is better than the riches of many wicked

schools.summary: Sharpens the warning to only evil can come of it, and reads the clause as standing alone: the fretting ends in the fretter's own sin, while those he makes himself like are cut off — it is the end, the final and consequently eternal end, that decides the matter. On the inheritance it renders heirs of the land and takes the land as Canaan, while a companion voice extends the promise from land to earth and hears the words already in the mouth of the Preacher on the Mount. The disappearance of the wicked is kept social — he has dropped out of his place, and his tribe knows him no more.

Refuses to read the vanishing of the wicked as annihilation: non-entities have no being anywhere, and these men die, rise at the last day and stand before the judgment seat; what ceases is only their flourishing presence in the world. Illustrates the recoiling sword from the death of Saul, and concedes the plain fact behind the closing proverb, that though some of the righteous have been rich, the wicked generally hold the larger share.

Insists the word rendered earth means land throughout the psalm and denotes Judea, so that the meek are the afflicted Jewish captives and the promise is of their return; reads the vanishing of the wicked as the fall of Babylon, an empire then in its splendour whose very site can no longer be identified. Adds that whatever a good man has has God's blessing in it, while even the blessings of the wicked are cursed. A second voice in the school treats the promise as largely fulfilled already in the church's state, and reads the peace attached to it as chiefly inward.

Calls anger here aggravated insanity and warns that fretfulness lies on the verge of great sin, many who indulged a murmuring disposition having come at last to sin outright. Explains the plotting from the enmity between the two seeds and the scheming from the subtlety of the serpent — if they cannot gnaw they will gnash, if they may not bite they will bark. On the closing proverb it hears an allusion to the noise of a multitude, the hurly-burly of riotous wealth against a quieter portion, and concludes that content finds much in little while for a wicked heart the whole world is too little.

positions.summary: The land of Judea, literally, as an inheritance restored to returning captives.
Canaan, with the promise widened and lifted by Christ's Beatitude, so that the contented servant of God possesses the earth more truly than its titled owners.
The land, and finally the earth: whatever self-love amasses falls at last to meekness that renounces earthly stays.
Largely a promise already fulfilled in the state of the church, with an inward peace as its principal content.

debates.question: What does it mean that the wicked shall not be?

positions.summary: Not annihilation, which is impossible; only the end of their presence and prosperity in this world, with judgment still to come.
A social vanishing: he has dropped out of his place, and those who knew him know him no longer.
A dated historical prophecy of the destruction of Babylon, whose site cannot now be found.

outliers.reading: Re-reads the psalm systematically as an exilic document, holding that the recurring word means land rather than earth throughout, that the meek are the Jewish captives, and that the wicked who cease to be are the Babylonian empire.

themes: Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil.
For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the Lord, they shall inherit the earth.
For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be.
But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.
The wicked plotteth against the just, and gnasheth upon him with his teeth.
The Lord shall laugh at him: for he seeth that his day is coming.
The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, and to slay such as be of upright conversation.
Their sword shall enter into their own heart, and their bows shall be broken.
A little that a righteous man hath is better than the riches of many wicked.

17.pericope_label: For the arms of the wicked shall be broken: but the Lord upholdeth the righteous... The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth

schools.summary: Distinguishes the broken arms as limbs of the body rather than the sword and bow of the previous verse, the contrast being with the arms of God under the righteous. Then makes the stretch's most restrictive claim: the everlasting inheritance here is not yet conceived as reaching into the future world as in the New Testament, and surviving the famine refers only to this present life. On the comparison drawn for God's enemies it argues that the words should now be rendered as the glory of the meadows, returning the psalm to the grass of its second verse, while a companion voice finds both senses of the smoke admissible and reads the unpaid debt as an old promise restated in proverbial form.

Divides the broken arm between the hand that can no longer strike and the substance in which the wicked trusted, and takes the perishing set against the righteous man's inheritance as eternal perdition rather than the death common to good and bad. On the unpaid debt it settles for disposition rather than incapacity: they do not pay because they will not, having taken no thought of it when they borrowed.

Reads the broken arms as power to do evil withdrawn, talents lent and abused being resumed, and keeps the exilic frame, hearing in the promise another indirect assurance of restoration. Reports that the comparison for God's enemies has troubled the critics, canvasses the versions that make them vanish like smoke as soon as they are exalted, and then follows the Hebrew to the fat of a sacrifice consumed on the altar. On the debt it holds both explanations at once and grounds the contrast in grace, mercy shown because mercy was received. A second voice takes the inheritance as passing to the righteous man's seed and, at death, exchanged for one infinitely better.

Supplies the epigram for the broken arms — God often makes implacable men incapable men — and asks what is more contemptible than toothless malice. On the unpaid debt it states the duty first, that it is not merely a shameful paltry thing but a sinful wicked thing not to repay what we have borrowed, then reports fairly the alternative that the verse describes misery rather than wickedness, and concludes that both are to be feared: a great sin in those able to deny their debts, a great misery in those unable to pay.

debates.question: What does the psalm mean by comparing God's enemies to the fat of lambs?

positions.summary: Sacrificial fat, wholly consumed by fire on the altar, so that they consume away in the fire of God's wrath.
Not fat at all but the glory of the meadows, a reading now generally allowed, which returns the psalm to its opening image of withering grass.
The point lies in the smoke rather than the fat: they are resolved into it, or go as smoke goes, thick at first and thinner until it is not there.

debates.question: Why does the wicked man borrow and not repay?

positions.summary: Because he will not — it is a disposition of the mind, not an inability.
Because he cannot: judgment has reduced him to a poverty in which he must borrow and can never repay.
Either, and both are miserable: he may refuse because he is wicked or fail because he is beggared.

outliers.reading: Denies that the psalm's everlasting inheritance yet reaches into a future world, restricting both it and the promise of survival in famine to this present life, and so declining the reading every other voice here assumes.

themes: For the arms of the wicked shall be broken: but the Lord upholdeth the righteous.
The Lord knoweth the days of the upright: and their inheritance shall be for ever.
They shall not be ashamed in the evil time: and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied.
But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the Lord shall be as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away.
The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.

22.pericope_label: For such as be blessed of him shall inherit the earth... The righteous shall inherit the land, and dwell therein for ever

schools.summary: Contests both the noun and the verb in the ordering of a man's steps: the steps are made firm, not directed as the Greek and Latin have it, and the noun means man in an ethical sense — while a companion voice reads the line generally, all stability in human conduct coming from divine guidance. On the psalmist's long observation it invokes the old rule that bodily promises are understood with the exception of the cross and chastisement, concedes that the psalm does not deny temporary forsakenness, and holds that it meets the doubt without knowledge of any final adjustment in a future world. It also identifies a missing stanza in the acrostic and proposes its restoration.

Keeps the ordered steps to the man already blessed, whose good conduct is not of himself, and reads the fall of the next verse as a fall into temptation and by it into sins, and great ones. Waits in the way of God's appointments, where the design of his providences and the end of the wicked can be learned, and takes the blessing named at the head of the stretch as the Lord's rather than the righteous man's.

Objects that nothing in the text answers to good: the noun means a strong man or hero, used to show that even the most powerful must be upheld. Denies flatly that the fall is a fall into sin — neither the text nor any version intimates it — citing an ancient version that reads it of sickness, and applies it to a people lying for a time under their adversaries. Affirms the long observation as literally true from personal experience, finds the twofold gift of grace in the closing exhortation, and reads the closing threat as judgments descending to posterity as mercies do.

Declines to repeat the psalmist's observation as its own, having relieved the children of undoubtedly good men who came as common mendicants, while defending the psalmist on the ground that his dispensation was more outward; then narrows the claim, one half of it a rule without exception and the other seldom broken. Calls the two halves of the closing exhortation the quintessence of the psalm — sin left as Lot left Sodom, without a backward look — and warns that the man who neglects to do good will soon fall into evil.

debates.question: Whose steps are ordered by the Lord?

positions.summary: The godly man's specifically, the noun carrying an emphatic ethical sense beyond the general proverb.
Any man's: the line states that all the stability there is in human conduct comes from God's guidance.
The strong man's — the word means a hero, and the point is that even the most powerful must be upheld or his strength avails little.

debates.question: Is it literally true that the righteous are never forsaken and their children never beg?

positions.summary: Yes, without exception, and confirmed by a lifetime's observation in several countries.
Not as it stands today: the first half is a rule without exception, the second only seldom broken, and the psalmist wrote under a more outward dispensation.
The temporal promises were more express to the Jews than they are to Christians.
The psalm never denied temporary destitution; it sets what abides against what is transitory, and its problem is fully solved only in the light of the New Testament.

outliers.reading: Identifies a whole stanza missing from the Hebrew acrostic, restores it from the Greek and Latin as the unjust shall be punished, and explains the loss as a scribe's confusion of two similar letters.

themes: For such as be blessed of him shall inherit the earth; and they that be cursed of him shall be cut off.
The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord: and he delighteth in his way.
Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the Lord upholdeth him with his hand.
I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.
He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed.
Depart from evil, and do good; and dwell for evermore.
For the Lord loveth judgment, and forsaketh not his saints; they are preserved for ever: but the seed of the wicked shall be cut off.
The righteous shall inherit the land, and dwell therein for ever.

30.pericope_label: The mouth of the righteous speaketh wisdom, and his tongue talketh of judgment... Wait on the Lord, and keep his way, and he shall exalt thee to inherit the land

schools.summary: States a principle about moral stability: the walk of the righteous has a fixed inward rule, the law being no external object of knowledge or compulsory precept but something in the heart, joined to the will as the motive of action because it is the law of the God he loves. Sets God's examination against the examination of men — if men judge the righteous the supreme Judge acquits — and reads the promise at the close as possession of the land from which the evildoers, who had carried themselves as its sole lords, are now cut off.

Reads the mouth's wisdom as meditation first and utterance second, ranging over the wisdom of God in creation and grace, Christ who is wisdom itself, and the gospel as ancient wisdom ordained before the world. Takes the law in the heart as the moral law written in Adam and obliterated by sin, reinscribed in regeneration, so that the man knows its spirituality, the impossibility of justification by it, and Christ as its fulfilling end. Waits in the way of God's appointments, where the design of his providences may be learned.

Says negatively what the others say positively — foolish and corrupt conversation cannot come out of such a mouth — and reads the law in the heart as the promised new covenant already fulfilled, the precepts written not only in the Bible but in the heart, which then dictates to eyes, mouth, hands and feet. Defines the waiting as keeping God's way and using his ordinances, and finds its picture in the verb, a straight line drawn from the human heart along its desire to God; keeps the exilic reading for the promise attached. A second voice glosses the sliding as swerving from the rule.

Explains why the psalm turns to speech here: a poem about the different fates of just and wicked needs a test by which they may be told apart, and the tongue is no ill index of character. Compresses the heart's furnishing to the best thing in the best place producing the best results. Divides waiting between duty, which is ours, and events, which are God's, so that we keep his way and attend the motions of providence — and calls waiting itself a lofty eminence, in obedience as a servant, in hope as an heir, in expectation as a believer.

debates.question: What is the law of God being in the heart?

positions.summary: The moral law, written in Adam and defaced by sin, reinscribed at regeneration according to the covenant promise.
The promised new covenant already fulfilled in this man, the precepts written in his heart as well as in his Bible.
A fixed inward rule that has ceased to be external or compulsory, joined to the will itself as the motive of action.

debates.question: What is promised to the man who waits and keeps God's way?

positions.summary: Restoration from exile: the captives lifted from their abject state to the land of their fathers, and shown the fall of the empire that held them.
Possession of the land from which the evildoers have been cut off.
All earthly good that is really good, and heavenly good without stint.

outliers.reading: Derives the whole meaning of waiting from the geometry of its verb, which he takes to imply a right line extended from one point to another — the heart the first point, its intense desire the line, and God the last.

themes: The mouth of the righteous speaketh wisdom, and his tongue talketh of judgment.
The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide.
The wicked watcheth the righteous, and seeketh to slay him.
The Lord will not leave him in his hand, nor condemn him when he is judged.
Wait on the Lord, and keep his way, and he shall exalt thee to inherit the land: when the wicked are cut off, thou shalt see it.

35.pericope_label: I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree... and he shall save them, because they trust in him

schools.summary: Refuses two received readings at once. The tree is taken as an oak or terebinth standing in its native soil from time immemorial, or, by a companion voice, as an unidentified indigenous evergreen — both rejecting the Greek and Latin alteration to cedars of Lebanon. The verb that follows, they insist, cannot mean that the man vanished, since that will not suit a tree; it says that one passed by. And the famous promise of a peaceful end is declared a mistranslation, the noun meaning posterity, so that what is promised the man of peace is descendants, while the posterity of the wicked is destroyed.

Is sure a particular man stands behind the picture, someone in great authority and formidable to all around, though it declines to name him. Mounts a long refusal of the word perfect: none are perfect in themselves, grace opens gradually, sin remains in the best of men, and no saint ever claimed perfection — leaving a perfection of parts rather than of degrees, and sincerity as the word's usual force. Restricts the destruction to obstinate transgressors, since all men are transgressors in Adam, and ends with a salvation of God only and entire.

Reads the whole passage as history: the great tree is the tree of Nebuchadnezzar's vision, and its passing away is the fall of Babylon. On the disputed promise it canvasses the versions and concludes that the original cannot possibly bear the received translation, preferring preserve innocence and keep equity in view, for the man of peace shall leave a numerous posterity. Grounds the closing salvation in the God who made them righteous by blotting out their sins, and reads the final clause practically, as faith and obedience kept in continual exercise. A second voice keeps the traditional sense, that all shall end well.

Treats the verse as an entry from the psalmist's diary and recommends the practice, since it would be well if we too took notes of providences; the man observed added house to house and field to field and seemed ever verdant like a laurel. On the destruction of the wicked it observes that nothing can be well which will undoubtedly end ill.

debates.question: What tree is the wicked man compared to?

positions.summary: An unidentified indigenous evergreen, possibly the sweet bay; no particular species need be intended.
An oak or terebinth grown gigantic over centuries in its native soil.
The great tree of Nebuchadnezzar's vision, whose head reached to heaven.

debates.question: Is the end of the perfect man peace, or posterity?

positions.summary: Posterity: the noun means descendants elsewhere and the parallelism decides it, so the familiar rendering is simply wrong.
Posterity, reached without disputing the text: the man of peace has a future in his children, while the apostates leave none.
Peace: though such a man meet troubles on his way, all shall end well.

outliers.reading: Turns the verse's call to mark the perfect man into a denial that any such man exists in the strict sense, redefining the word as sincerity and allowing only a perfection of parts and not of degrees.

themes: I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree.
Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found.
Mark the perfect man, and behold the upright: for the end of that man is peace.
But the transgressors shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off.
But the salvation of the righteous is of the Lord: he is their strength in the time of trouble.
And the Lord shall help them, and deliver them: he shall deliver them from the wicked, and save them, because they trust in him.
